summary: A speculative news-style feature on how anti-gravity technology moves from lab to everyday life. It traces the Overton Engine's 2024 unveiling in Zurich, the 2025 breakthrough in generating a gravitational null field, and the market growth, public adoption in Singapore and consumer cars that followed. It closes with a human-interest story of a long-distance couple whose relationship is helped by anti-gravity travel.
one_line: A news feature charting anti-gravity transportation from the 2024 Overton Engine demo to mass adoption by 2029, and its effects on economies and relationships.
key_facts: In November 2024, the Overton Institute's headquarters in Zurich hosted the unveiling of the Overton Engine, led by Dr. Eva Schneider and her team.
The prototype vehicle, nicknamed the "Levitator," hovered a few feet above the ground and performed complex maneuvers silently during the demonstration.
In September 2025, a consortium of engineers led by Dr. Eva Schneider and Dr. Akira Yamamoto, a physicist based in Tokyo, identified a stable method for generating a gravitational null field.
The technology required a balance between electro-magnetic fields and superconducting materials, and advances in quantum computing and material sciences enabled the breakthrough.
Earliest prototypes used large, cumbersome rigs and could hover only a few inches off the ground; within a year the Overton Engine was compact enough for personal vehicles.
By December 2026, significant capital was flowing into the anti-gravity market, and the International Transportation Safety Board established global standards and safety protocols.
On April 1, 2027, Singapore announced it would integrate anti-gravity technology into its public transportation system, promising reduced emissions, noise pollution and traffic congestion.
Celestia, a startup co-founded by Jasmine Patel and Luis Dominguez, aimed to make anti-gravity personal transportation accessible to the middle class.
Celestia's affordable model became an overnight sensation upon release in August 2028.
By mid-2029, luxury car manufacturers were offering elite anti-gravity marques to the wealthy.
In fall 2029, Samuel Ito (robotics engineer in Los Angeles) and Meena Ito (climate scientist in Oslo) became one of the first couples to own a consumer anti-gravity car.
The Itos' car let them make frequent weekend visits, closing the 5,400-mile gap between them.
